nameStory: Temple juniper gets its name from its sacred status in East Asian cultures, where it's traditionally planted around Buddhist and Shinto temples. The species name 'rigida' means 'rigid' in Latin, referring to its stiff, sharply pointed needles that feel almost prickly to the touch.
description: Temple juniper is a medium-sized evergreen tree with a distinctive upright, narrow shape when young that becomes more open and irregular with age. This Asian native can grow 20-30 feet tall in New England's climate, though it stays smaller than in its homeland. Its most striking feature is its extremely sharp, needle-like leaves that stick out in all directions from the branches, giving it a somewhat wild, unkempt appearance compared to other junipers.

idTips.label: Needles
idTips.description: Sharp, rigid needles about half an inch long that jut out from branches at all angles - they're so stiff and pointed they can actually prick your finger if you're not careful

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Reddish-brown bark that peels off in thin, fibrous strips, revealing lighter patches underneath - you can often pull these strips away with your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Young trees grow in a narrow, upright column, but mature specimens develop an irregular, somewhat scraggly outline with drooping branch tips

idTips.label: Cones
idTips.description: Small, dark blue to black berry-like cones about a quarter-inch across that often have a whitish, waxy bloom on their surface

idTips.label: Branch Pattern
idTips.description: Branches tend to droop slightly at the tips, and the overall branching pattern looks more irregular and loose than other junipers

habitat: In New England, temple juniper is extremely rare and found almost exclusively in cultivated settings like arboretums, botanical gardens, or as ornamental plantings around buildings. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun, tolerating poor soils better than many other conifers.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears as bright green tips on branch ends, contrasting with the darker older foliage.
seasonality.summer: Foliage reaches its darkest green color, and small inconspicuous flowers may appear on mature trees.
seasonality.fall: Berry-like cones ripen to dark blue-black if present, and foliage may take on slightly purplish tints.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen needles provide year-round identification opportunities, and the tree's irregular silhouette stands out against snow.

funFact: Temple juniper is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only twice by nature observers - making it more elusive than some endangered native species, despite being perfectly hardy in our climate!
confusionNotes: The extremely sharp, rigid needles that stick out at all angles make temple juniper nearly impossible to confuse with other junipers once you feel them - common juniper has softer needles, and eastern redcedar has scale-like leaves rather than true needles.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, temple juniper is a true juniper, not a cedar - like many conifers, it suffers from naming confusion since early settlers called many evergreen trees 'cedar.' In its native range across East Asia, this tree can live for centuries and is considered a symbol of endurance.
compareHints: Temple juniper stands apart from New England's other junipers by its uniquely rigid, sharply pointed needles that radiate in all directions from the branches. Eastern redcedar has scale-like leaves pressed against the twigs, while common juniper has softer needles in whorls of three, and creeping juniper grows as a low groundcover rather than an upright tree.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike common juniper which stays low and shrubby with only needle-like leaves, eastern redcedar grows into a proper tree with both needle and scale foliage.

Common juniper is easily distinguished from eastern redcedar by its low, spreading growth habit (redcedar grows tall and upright) and its sharp needle-like leaves (redcedar has scale-like leaves that lie flat against branches).
Unlike eastern redcedar which grows tall and upright, or common juniper which forms low but upright shrubs, creeping juniper is the only New England juniper that truly grows flat along the ground.
Japanese garden juniper is much lower and more spreading than eastern redcedar, which grows as an upright tree.
